# Exact interval source cost for every multiplicity

Let k be a positive integer. For a positive-length interval B, let
0<=eta<=1_B dx have mass alpha |B|, where 0<=alpha<=1, and let g be
the centroid of

    rho=1_B dx+k eta.

The true k-source average indicator implication controls
|B intersect H|+eta(H), with ONE eta copy. It does not control the
density cap mass rho(H)=|B intersect H|+k eta(H). This note determines
the sharp infimum of the former cost, divided by |B|, for all closed
halfspaces of the line containing g, all B, and all such eta.
Call that infimum Psi_(1,k)(alpha). All minima below are attained by
indicator submeasures on one or two subintervals; no limit or numerical
optimization is needed.

## 1. Exact formula

For k=1,

    Psi_(1,1)(alpha)=(1+alpha^2)/2.                    (1)

For every integer k>=2, define

    L_k=[sqrt((k+1)/3)-1]/k,
    U_k=[sqrt(k(k+1))-1]/k.

Then 0<=L_k<U_k<1, and

    Psi_(1,k)(alpha)
      =alpha+(1+k alpha^2)/[2(1+k alpha)],       0<=alpha<=L_k;

      =[2sqrt((1+k alpha)^2+k+1)-3-k alpha]/k,
                                               L_k<=alpha<=U_k;

      =[k alpha^2-(k-1)alpha+k]/(k+1),           U_k<=alpha<=1.
                                                               (2)

The overlapping endpoint expressions agree. At alpha=0 the answer is
1/2; at alpha=1 it is one, since the source cost is twice ordinary
volume at the interval midpoint. The k=2 formula recovers the independently
derived square-root and saturated-band branches with crossover
U_2=(sqrt(6)-1)/2; its first branch consists only of alpha=0.

## 2. Exact scalar feasible set

Normalize B=[0,1]. Orient the chosen cap toward 1 and first move its
boundary to the actual centroid; this can only decrease its source
cost. Write

    s=|B intersect H|, r=eta(H).

The elementary domination constraints are

    0<=r<=min(alpha,s), s+alpha-r<=1.                 (3)

In upper-tail rank v=1-x, uniform volume is uniform on [0,1]. Among
dominated densities with mass r on [0,s] and alpha-r on [s,1], the
first v-moment is minimized by filling

    [0,r] union [s,s+alpha-r].                        (4)

This follows by subtracting the two interval indicators and their
cutoff values from the increasing integrand v; the remaining products
are nonnegative on both sides of each cutoff. The exact centroid
equation and this moment bound give

    2(1+k alpha)s
       >=1+k[r^2+(s+alpha-r)^2-s^2].                 (5)

Conversely, at equality in (5), the indicator bands (4) put the rho
centroid exactly at x=1-s, realizing the source cost s+r. For purposes
of minimizing s+r, every minimizer of the compact feasible set (3),(5)
has equality in (5): if it were strict, decrease s and r together
when r>0, or decrease s alone when r=0. All constraints persist for
a sufficiently small decrement and the cost strictly decreases.
Feasibility at s=1,r=alpha and infeasibility at s=0 justify compact
attainment and the small-decrement argument. The last constraint is
strict at s=1,r=alpha for every k>=1, so a minimizer has 0<s<1.

Thus the scalar characterization and the band constructions are exact
for the full interval problem, rather than just necessary inequalities.

## 3. One-variable minimization and every feasibility boundary

Expanding (5) gives s>=S(r), where

    S(r)=[1+k alpha^2-2k alpha r+2kr^2]/[2(1+kr)].    (6)

The necessary upper constraint S(r)<=1-alpha+r is equivalent to

    r>=r_0:=[k alpha^2+2alpha-1]/[2(k+1)].            (7)

Hence every feasible pair has r in [max(0,r_0),alpha] and cost at
least F(r)=S(r)+r. Its derivative is

    F'(r)
      =[4(1+kr)^2-D]/[2(1+kr)^2],
    D=(1+k alpha)^2+k+1.                             (8)

The only root is

    r_*=(sqrt(D)-2)/(2k),                            (9)

with the derivative negative below it and positive above it. These
identities give the minimum on the necessary interval by clipping
r_* to that interval; the next checks prove the resulting point is
genuinely feasible, including the lower constraint s>=r.

For k>=2, r_*>=0. Direct squaring of positive quantities gives

    r_*<=alpha  iff alpha>=L_k,
    r_*>=r_0   iff alpha<=U_k.                       (10)

Here r_0 is nonpositive until
A_k=(sqrt(k+1)-1)/k, and L_k<=A_k<=U_k. The minimizing r is therefore

    r=alpha below L_k,
    r=r_* between L_k and U_k,
    r=r_0 above U_k.                                 (11)

All three choices satisfy 0<=r<=alpha and r>=r_0. To check S(r)>=r:

- In the first branch, this is 1-2alpha-k alpha^2>=0, which follows
  from alpha<=L_k<=A_k.
- In the middle branch define R_0=(1+k alpha^2)/[2(1+k alpha)].
  Then S(r)>=r exactly when r<=R_0. Writing A=1+k alpha gives
  1+kR_0=D/(2A)>sqrt(D)/2=1+kr_*, since D>A^2. Thus r_*<R_0.
- In the last branch S(r_0)=1-alpha+r_0>=r_0.

The constraint S(r)<=1-alpha+r follows from (7), and S(r)>0 is
immediate from the numerator 1+k(alpha-r)^2+kr^2 in (6). It follows
that every pair s=S(r), r in (11) obeys all of (3). These points attain
the lower bound furnished by the one-variable minimization, so no
other feasible branch has been discarded.

Substitution of (11) into F gives the three formulas (2). For the
middle one, put t=1+kr. Then

    F(r)=[D/t+4t-6-2k alpha]/(2k),

and t=sqrt(D)/2 at r=r_*. In the final branch use
F(r_0)=1-alpha+2r_0.

For k=1, the sign changes of r_0 and r_* coincide at
alpha=sqrt(2)-1. Below this value r=0 is optimal; above it r=r_0
is optimal. The same feasibility checks apply, and both costs simplify
to (1+alpha^2)/2. This proves (1) separately without applying the
nonnegative-L_k formulas outside their stated range.

## 4. Exact minimum over the added mass

For k>=2, the minimum over alpha in [0,1] is uniquely attained at
alpha=L_k, and equals

    min_alpha Psi_(1,k)(alpha)
       =[sqrt(3(k+1))-2]/k.                           (12)

Indeed the derivative in the first branch has sign
3(1+k alpha)^2-(k+1), and is nonpositive up to L_k. The derivative
of the middle branch is

    2(1+k alpha)/sqrt((1+k alpha)^2+k+1)-1,

which is nonnegative from L_k onward, and positive beyond L_k.
The derivative of the last branch is [2k alpha-(k-1)]/(k+1),
positive for alpha>=U_k because
sqrt(k(k+1))>(k+1)/2 for k>=1. The endpoints agree, proving the
unique minimum. At L_k, writing m=sqrt((k+1)/3) gives
r=alpha=(m-1)/k and s=(2m-1)/k, hence (12).

For k=1 the minimum is 1/2 at alpha=0. Formula (12) is not asserted
for k=1. In all cases the asymptotic scale for large multiplicity is
k^(-1/2), rather than a positive universal constant.

## 5. A fully rational obstruction to any multiplier uniform in k

For every integer m>=2, take

    k=3m^2-1, alpha=(m-1)/k,
    B=[0,1], eta=1_[1-alpha,1] dx.                   (13)

Then 1+k alpha=m, and a direct first-moment calculation gives

    g=[1/2+k alpha(1-alpha/2)]/(1+k alpha),
    1-g=(2m-1)/k.                                    (14)

The closed upper halfspace H=[g,infinity) contains the full eta band,
since 1-g>=alpha. Therefore its ACTUAL source cost is exactly

    |B intersect H|+eta(H)=(3m-2)/(3m^2-1).           (15)

Comparing to gamma_1(|B|+eta(B))=(1+alpha)/2 gives the exact ratio

    2(3m-2)/(3m^2+m-2)<=2/m.                         (16)

The comparison follows by cross multiplication from 3m-2>=0.
For any proposed positive constant c independent of multiplicity,
choose an integer m>2/c. Equation (16) contradicts the bound
source_cost>=c gamma_d(|B|+eta(B)) already in dimension d=1.

All bodies, densities, centroids and halfspace thresholds in (13)--(16)
are rational, and the halfspace is closed and passes through the actual
centroid. This is a certificate, not an asymptotic numerical example.
It rules out a constant uniform in BOTH k and dimension, and in fact
already one uniform in k with dimension fixed at one. It does not rule
out constants depending on a fixed k.

The density cap mass in this example is instead
rho(H)=(2m-1)/k+(m-1). Replacing the source cost by that expression
would change the problem and erase the obstruction.

## 6. Boundary conventions and scope

The formulas apply to positive integer k and positive-length intervals.
All halfspace boundaries have zero measure. Alpha=0, alpha=1 and the
two branch junctions were included explicitly. If multiplicity zero
is desired separately, its uniform midpoint gives sharp source cost
Psi_(1,0)(alpha)=max(1/2,alpha), by filling the opposite half first.
For a zero-dimensional singleton, the source cost is simply 1+alpha
under counting measure, independently of k; no interval formula is
used in that case.

This note concerns weighted-centroid source certificates. It does not
assert a bad mixed-integer body, nor rule out selecting different actual
centers by another construction. In particular the large-k obstruction
does not contradict OC, which has no multiplicity parameter k.
